title: The Slate Sings
passages:
The ore stub at Anza had four lamps and three of them had been dead since spring, which suited Doan fine. Their shift had ended at six and never started again — clearance withdrawn, the board said, in the flat way the board said things — so they had come out to the stub with their wrist looped twice in the overlap locker's own cord and nothing at all to do. The overlap locker was the steel box at the stub that held the key a loader used to cover two shifts at once; the latch wouldn't take their thumb anymore, so they'd taken the cord instead. A dead key was still theirs. And Doan, who had carried eleven seals' worth of somebody else's food down the ore line without once asking what the seals were for, had decided around four that morning that this was the year they asked about everything.

Then the rail started to hum. Not a chime, not a horn. Just the low note the ore line makes when something heavy comes down it slow.

It came in dark. Every rig on the Interior runs with a transponder — a box that tells the board who it is and where it is, and blinks a green lamp at the node so the yard knows to open a gate. This one had a bracket where the box should have been and nothing in the bracket but frost. It was a tender, Doan could see that much: a short rig, built to carry a crew and a water tank instead of freight. Its deck was empty and swept. No canister cradles, no receiving jaw marks, nothing on it a person could stamp.

It stopped on the stub mark without asking for a berth. Rigs chime when they want one. That's the whole arrangement. This one just sat there breathing cold.

Doan keyed the handheld. "Anza ore stub to inbound. You're dark and you're on my rails. Say a name."

The yard channel — the open channel every rig answers on when it wants something — gave back carrier hiss and nothing else.

"Great. Chatty." Doan walked a wide circle around it, cord swinging, and checked the stub reader on its post, the plate where an inbound rig says its name so the node can log it. Blank. Reader two, up in Teodoro's shop, was a different animal; that one read badges and plates and people, and Doan had no standing to be near it.

"Nour," they said into the handheld. "Ore stub. There's a tender sitting on my rails with no transponder and no post."

A pause, and the board ledge's particular silence behind her. "Then it isn't on my board and it isn't my problem."

"Bold. That's your whole personality, you know that?"

"It's kept this node eating." Another pause, and her voice came down. "Did it chime?"

"No."

"Don't touch it." Nour said it fast, the way she said things she'd already decided to be right about. "If that's coast, it's going to want a name off you, and you don't have one that's yours anymore. Get inside, Doan."

Doan looked at the empty deck, at the tank, at the swept plate where a crew should have been standing with their hands in their pockets.

"It's not coast," they said. "Coast knocks."

They put the handheld away and stood in the dark with a dead key on their wrist and did the thing they'd been avoiding since six that morning, which was think about the seals. Eleven short across four runs, all stamped Bay 4 Shift 2, all going down the line to a station that ate well. Doan had handed those canisters off and taken the roster weight for it and never asked a single question, because asking was how you lost the fat shift.

A tender with an empty deck had nothing to stamp. That was what sat wrong. Whatever this was, it hadn't come for the food.

Something inside the hull let go — a latch, heavy, unhurried. A seam of yellow light opened along the flank, and a step folded down onto the frozen stub with a sound like a dropped wrench.

Doan didn't move. "Well," they said. "Nobody ever just knocks."
